headline: Where Lindt's cocoa comes from, and what the public record says about it
summary: Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire grow more than half of the world's cocoa, and US Department of Labor-funded research found about 1.56 million children in cocoa child labor there in 2018/19. In July 2026 a complaint was moved to a Washington, DC federal court alleging that Lindt & Sprüngli misled consumers about its efforts to end child labor in its supply chain. Lindt denies the allegations. This project maps how cocoa from the region reaches US shelves under Lindt, Ghirardelli and Russell Stover, using only public sources. It maps sector-level risk and the gap between public claims and documented conditions. It does not say any specific product was made with child labor.

lawsuit.relief: Per ConfectioneryNews, the case seeks changes to marketing claims rather than damages.

pairs.allegation: The complaint alleges Lindt misleads consumers by saying it is trying to eliminate child labor and is committed to human rights.
pairs.response: Lindt denies the allegations, says it strongly condemns all forms of child labor, has supplier protocols and systematically investigates suspected cases.

pairs.allegation: It alleges Lindt has known for more than 20 years that its cocoa is produced using child labor.
pairs.response: Lindt denies this. It points to its Farming Program, unannounced farm visits and a goal of monitoring-system coverage for all cocoa from risk countries.

pairs.allegation: It targets certification labels and sourcing claims on packaging.
pairs.response: Lindt says all its cocoa is sourced as Rainforest Alliance Certified from 2026, that the seal is being introduced gradually, and that it invests beyond certification. (This June 2026 release predates the suit and is not a direct reply to it.)

pairs.allegation: The case seeks to stop what the plaintiff calls misleading representations, not money damages.
pairs.response: Lindt called the claims misguided and noted the same group has sued other chocolate companies (as relayed by press; not independently verified here).

steps: Collected public sources only: government pages, company releases, news reports, court-docket aggregators.
Every record carries a source URL, date accessed and a confidence label.
Facts were paraphrased, not copied. The lawsuit's claims are shown as allegations next to Lindt's denial.
Network edges between suppliers and factories are marked Unverified unless a source names both ends.
Free tools used: web search, DOL/USITC portals, Lindt's own publications, ImportYeti, CourtListener, OpenSanctions.

about.text: This is an independent open-source-intelligence portfolio project. It was built to show how a public-source supply-chain map can be assembled with free tools, how claims are separated from evidence, and where commercial data would add value. It has no connection to Lindt, International Rights Advocates or any party to the case.

legal: Independent research from public sources. Not legal advice. Statements about the lawsuit are allegations only; Lindt denies them. No product is claimed to be made with child labor. Corrections welcome via GitHub issues.
